question: What is the first thing a rider should do to make sure a motorcycle won't let them down?
choice_a: Pick a motorcycle based only on color and style
choice_b: Buy the most powerful engine available
choice_c: Choose the motorcycle with the largest fuel tank
choice_d: Start with the right motorcycle for you -- one that fits you well
explanation: To make sure your motorcycle won't let you down, start with the right motorcycle for you -- it should fit you well, and you should read the owner's manual and be familiar with the controls.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.4, 'Know Your Motorcycle'

question: For a motorcycle to fit a rider well, the manual says:
choice_a: The rider's feet should reach the ground while seated, and the controls should be easy to operate
choice_b: The rider's feet should never touch the ground
choice_c: Only the taller of two riders should be able to reach the controls
choice_d: Fit is irrelevant as long as the motorcycle is street-legal
explanation: Your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate; smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners to operate.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.4, 'The Right Motorcycle For You'

question: At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should be equipped with all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: At a minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should have a headlight, taillight and brake light, front and rear brakes, turn signals, a horn, and two mirrors. A passenger backrest is not listed as minimum required equipment.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.4, 'The Right Motorcycle For You'

question: According to the manual, more than half of all crashes involve riders with how much experience on their motorcycle?
explanation: More than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle, so extra caution is urged for any new or unfamiliar machine.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.5, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: If you lend your motorcycle to a friend, the manual advises that you should:
choice_a: Only lend it if it has a full tank of gas
choice_b: Never explain the controls, since experienced riders don't need it
choice_c: Remove the mirrors first for safety
choice_d: Make sure they are licensed and know how to ride before letting them out into traffic
explanation: If you lend your motorcycle to friends, make sure they are licensed and know how to ride before allowing them out into traffic; crashes are more likely among beginning riders and on unfamiliar machines.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.5, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: Before riding an unfamiliar motorcycle, a rider should find and be able to operate which items without having to look for them?
choice_a: Turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve, and engine cut-off switch
choice_d: Nothing in particular -- all motorcycles are identical to operate
explanation: If using an unfamiliar motorcycle, find out where everything is -- particularly the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve, and engine cut-off switch -- and find and operate them without having to look.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.5, 'Get Familiar with the Motorcycle Controls'

question: What is the T-CLOCS pre-ride inspection reminder used for?
choice_a: A once-a-year inspection performed only by a licensed dealer
choice_b: A quick, routine check of critical motorcycle components that should be done before every ride
choice_c: A checklist used only when purchasing a used motorcycle
choice_d: A test given only to riders under 18
explanation: T-CLOCS is a convenient reminder developed by the Motorcycle Safety Foundation; a T-CLOCS inspection only takes a few minutes and should be conducted before every ride to prevent problems.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: In the T-CLOCS acronym, what does the "T" stand for?
explanation: T-CLOCS stands for Tires and Wheels, Controls, Lights and Electrics, Oil and Other Fluids, Chassis, and Stands.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: When checking tires and wheels during a T-CLOCS inspection, a rider should check tire inflation pressure, treadwear, sidewall condition, and:
choice_a: Nothing else -- tires only need a visual glance
choice_b: The color of the tire sidewalls only
choice_d: That the front and rear brake levers each feel firm and hold the motorcycle when fully applied
explanation: Under Tires and Wheels, check inflation pressure, treadwear, and sidewall/tread condition, and try the front and rear brake levers one at a time to make sure each feels firm and holds the motorcycle when fully applied.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'T -- Tires and Wheels'

question: During the "Controls" step of a T-CLOCS check, the throttle should:
choice_a: Snap back to fully closed when released
choice_b: Stay wherever it is left, with no spring return
choice_c: Feel loose and require no effort to twist
choice_d: Only be tested by a mechanic, never the rider
explanation: Make sure the clutch and throttle operate smoothly; the throttle should snap back to fully closed when released, and the clutch should feel tight and operate smoothly.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'C -- Controls'

question: During the "Lights and Electrics" step of a T-CLOCS check, a rider should test the headlight switch to confirm:
choice_b: Both high and low beams work
choice_d: The horn is louder than the taillight
explanation: Check both headlight and taillight, and test the switch to make sure both high and low beams work; also turn on both turn signals and try both brakes to make sure each turns on the brake light.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'L -- Lights and Electrics'

question: When adjusting mirrors as part of a pre-ride check, a mirror is properly adjusted when it shows:
choice_a: The front tire, to judge lean angle
choice_b: Only the sky, to avoid glare
choice_c: The lane behind and the lane next to you, even if it shows the edge of your arm or shoulder
choice_d: Nothing behind the rider at all
explanation: Adjust each mirror so you can see the lane behind and the lane next to you. When properly adjusted, a mirror may show the edge of your arm or shoulder -- but it's the road behind and to the side that matter.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'L -- Lights and Electrics'

question: During the "Oil and Other Fluids" step, what should a rider check underneath the motorcycle?
choice_c: The condition of the seat foam
choice_d: Signs of an oil or fuel leak
explanation: Check engine oil and transmission fluid levels, check brake hydraulic fluid and coolant weekly, and look underneath the motorcycle for signs of an oil or fuel leak.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.6, 'O -- Oil and Other Fluids'

question: During the "Stands" step of a T-CLOCS inspection, the center stand (if equipped) should:
choice_a: Be held firmly against the frame whenever the motorcycle is moving
choice_b: Always be left extended while riding
choice_d: Only be used for long-term storage
explanation: Ensure the side stand operates smoothly and its spring holds it tightly in the up position; if equipped, the center stand should also be held firmly against the frame whenever the motorcycle is moving.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.7, 'S -- Stands'

question: The manual explains that the word "accident" implies:
choice_a: That no rider is ever responsible for a crash
choice_b: An unforeseen event without fault, but in traffic most crash-involved people share some responsibility for what happened
choice_c: That only the other driver can ever be at fault
choice_d: An event that can never be prevented by rider awareness
explanation: "Accident" implies an unforeseen event that occurs without fault or negligence, but in traffic that is not the case -- most people involved in a crash should probably claim some responsibility for what takes place.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.7, 'Know Your Responsibilities'

question: Since a rider can't be sure other operators will see them or yield the right of way, the manual recommends riders lessen crash risk by doing all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: Communicating intentions with signals, brake light, and lane position
choice_b: Being visible through proper clothing, headlight use, and lane position
choice_c: Assuming eye contact from another driver guarantees they will yield
choice_d: Maintaining an adequate space cushion and searching 12 seconds ahead
explanation: To lessen the chances of a crash, riders should be visible, communicate intentions, maintain a space cushion, search 12 seconds ahead, identify hazards, and be prepared to act -- never assume eye contact guarantees another driver will yield.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.7, 'Know Your Responsibilities'

question: Who does the manual say ultimately bears responsibility for keeping from being the cause of, or an unprepared participant in, a crash?
choice_a: No one -- crashes are considered unavoidable
choice_d: Each individual rider, regardless of who else may share fault
explanation: Blame doesn't matter when someone is injured in a crash. It is up to each rider to keep from being the cause of, or an unprepared participant in, any crash.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.7, 'Know Your Responsibilities'
